title: Checking equation homogeneity

learning_outcomes.text: use SI base units to check the homogeneity of physical equations

prior_knowledge_summary: Force, energy and power can be written as kg m s^-2, kg m^2 s^-2 and kg m^2 s^-3.
A supplied relationship can be rearranged to find the SI base-unit form of an unfamiliar constant.
Products and quotients of units can be simplified by collecting powers of kg, m, s, A and K.
new_learning: An equation is homogeneous only when both sides, and every term joined by addition or subtraction, reduce to the same SI base-unit form.
A homogeneity check can reject an equation with incompatible units, identify a required unit or power, and show when a coefficient is dimensionless.
Matching units are necessary for a physical equation but do not prove that the equation is physically correct.
not_yet_taught: Precision, accuracy, resolution and uncertainty calculations.
Applications belonging to later Physics topics beyond supplied unit-analysis contexts.

visual_planning.reason: Six visuals create the opening contradiction, model a term-by-term unit ledger, show two complete checks, expose a misleading matching-units claim and summarise the decision route.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: Can an equation fail before any numbers are used?
content: A design card claims that a distance x is given by x = vt + at. The card says v has unit m s^-1, a has unit m s^-2 and t has unit s. No measurements are available. Can we still find a problem?
The first term vt has unit m. The second term at has unit m s^-1. A distance cannot equal a sum whose terms have different units. The equation fails before any value is substituted.
This is the power of a homogeneity check. It tests the unit structure of an equation.

figure.purpose: Create a contradiction by placing incompatible unit cards inside one proposed equation
figure.brief: Draw a white-paper teacher sketch of x = vt + at. Place a small m card under x and vt, and a contrasting m s^-1 card under at. Add the question can these be added? Do not show a corrected equation.
figure.alt_text: A proposed distance equation has metre units under one term and metre per second units under another, raising a question about adding them.

blocks.title: What a homogeneity check compares
content: Replace every quantity by its SI base-unit form. Ignore pure numbers such as 2 or pi because they have no unit. Keep any stated constant and its unit in the check.
Then simplify each complete term separately. Terms joined by multiplication belong together. Terms joined by plus or minus must be checked one by one before they are combined.
An equation is homogeneous when every term reduces to the same powers of the same base units. If even one power differs, the equation is not homogeneous.
Use a unit ledger: one row for each term and one column for kg, m, s, A and K. This prevents a matching factor from hiding a mismatched power.

figure.purpose: Make the term-by-term and base-unit-by-base-unit comparison explicit
figure.brief: Create a colourful hand-drawn unit ledger. Use rows labelled left side, first right term and second right term. Use columns kg, m, s, A and K with simple exponent boxes. Leave the exponents as symbols rather than giving a practice answer.
figure.alt_text: A unit ledger compares the exponent of each SI base unit for every term in an equation.

blocks.title: A complete check with three matching terms
content: Consider the supplied model E = Cmv^2 + Fd. For this unit exercise, E is energy, m is mass, v is speed, F is force, d is distance and C has no unit. We are checking only the units in the supplied model.
The left side has unit [E] = kg m^2 s^-2. For the first right-hand term, [Cmv^2] = 1 x kg x (m s^-1)^2 = kg m^2 s^-2.
For the second right-hand term, [Fd] = (kg m s^-2)(m) = kg m^2 s^-2. All three terms reduce to the same base-unit form, so the equation is homogeneous.
The check is independent of the numerical value of C. If C is dimensionless, changing C changes the size of the term but not its units.

figure.purpose: Show a complete homogeneous comparison across a left side and two added terms
figure.brief: Draw three horizontal calculation strips for E, Cmv^2 and Fd. Expand each to kg m^2 s^-2 using different colours for mass, length and time powers. End with three aligned matching cards and the word homogeneous.
figure.alt_text: Three unit calculations for energy and two right-hand terms all finish as kilogram metre squared per second squared.

blocks.title: Use homogeneity to find a missing power
content: A supplied model is R = M L^n / t^2. R has unit kg m s^-2, M has unit kg, L has unit m, t has unit s and n is unknown.
Substitute the units without guessing n: kg m s^-2 = kg m^n s^-2. The kg and s powers already match.
Compare the metre powers. The left side contains m^1, so n = 1. Substituting n = 1 gives kg m s^-2 on both sides.
The short route was to compare one exponent. The full substitution at the end is an independent check that no other base-unit power was overlooked.

figure.purpose: Teach unknown-power matching without hiding the unchanged base-unit powers
figure.brief: Create a four-line annotated notebook layout for R = ML^n/t^2, its base-unit substitution, the comparison 1 = n and the final whole-equation check. Highlight only the metre exponent comparison while leaving kg and s visibly matched.
figure.alt_text: An annotated unit derivation finds an unknown length exponent by comparing metre powers and then checks the whole equation.

blocks.title: A coefficient may need no unit
content: A device model is P = C rho A u^3. P is power, rho has unit kg m^-3, A has unit m^2, u has unit m s^-1 and C is a coefficient with an unknown unit.
Expand the factors without C: [rho A u^3] = (kg m^-3)(m^2)(m^3 s^-3) = kg m^2 s^-3.
This already matches the power unit kg m^2 s^-3. Therefore C needs no unit. It is dimensionless for this equation to be homogeneous.
If the product without C had reduced to a different unit, C would need the quotient [P]/[rho A u^3]. A coefficient is not automatically dimensionless.

figure.purpose: Show how a dimensionless coefficient is concluded rather than assumed
figure.brief: Draw a factor chain for rho, A and u cubed, with their base-unit cards combining to kg m^2 s^-3. Place the same power-unit card on the left, then show an empty unit tag beside C labelled no unit needed. Avoid numerical values.
figure.alt_text: Density, area and speed cubed combine to the unit of power, so the coefficient needs no unit.

blocks.title: Matching units do not prove the physics
content: It is tempting to say that a homogeneous equation must be correct. The reasoning feels strong because a unit mismatch can definitely expose a failure.

But many different expressions can have the same units. Both mv^2 and Fd have energy units, yet unit matching alone cannot tell whether either expression models a particular situation or whether a numerical factor is correct.

Use careful language. A mismatch proves that the equation cannot be correct as written. A match shows only that the equation passes the homogeneity check. Physical principles and evidence are still needed.

figure.purpose: Separate the strong conclusion from a unit mismatch from the limited conclusion of a unit match
figure.brief: Draw a two-branch teacher sketch. A red mismatch branch ends at cannot be correct as written. A green match branch ends at passes the unit check, then continues to a question mark labelled physics still needed. Keep the statements large and clear.
figure.alt_text: A decision sketch shows that mismatched units reject an equation, while matched units only pass the unit test and do not prove the physics.

blocks.title: A reliable homogeneity route
content: First separate every term joined by plus or minus. Second replace each quantity and stated constant with its SI base-unit form. Treat pure numbers as dimensionless.

Third simplify each term completely. Fourth compare the powers of every base unit. If a power is unknown, equate the matching exponents. If a constant is unknown, find the unit that completes the match.

Finally state the conclusion precisely: homogeneous, not homogeneous, or homogeneous only if a stated power or constant has the derived value. Remember that a match is a necessary check, not proof of the physical model.
The opening card fails because vt has unit m while at has unit m s^-1. We can reject it without entering the later study of motion.

concepts_taught: homogeneity requires matching SI base-unit powers on both sides and in every additive term
dimensionless numbers and coefficients do not change a term's units
matching units are necessary but do not prove that a physical equation is correct
misconceptions_addressed: only the two sides need comparison even when one side contains a sum
every coefficient must have a unit
a homogeneous equation is guaranteed to be physically correct
skills_students_can_now_use: reduce every term of a supplied equation to SI base units
decide whether a supplied equation is homogeneous
use homogeneity to determine an unknown exponent or the required unit of a constant
identify when a coefficient is dimensionless
state the limited conclusion supported by a successful homogeneity check
next_lesson_can_assume: SI base-unit powers can be compared term by term to check equation homogeneity
an unknown power or constant unit can be derived by matching base-unit exponents
matching units do not by themselves prove a physical model
